intro: This is the Rondo-Finale (Allegro) of Mahler’s Symphony No. 5, which ends in D major. The movement includes a horn tune, chasing string parts and a large brass chorale, and material from the preceding Adagietto returns in it as a dance.

cues.title: Opening of the finale, held A
cues.text: The horn holds an A, and the first violins hold it too, pp, dying away. Bassoon, oboe and clarinet play short phrases around it, the oboe marked zögernd (hesitating).
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183: Allegro; first horn lang, verklingend; first violins pp lang, verklingend; bassoon f, oboe p zögernd, clarinet Etwas langsamer. Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has the bassoon fragment sound only a few seconds into the movement: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Source of the bassoon phrase
cues.text: The bassoon’s short phrase comes from Mahler’s Wunderhorn song Lob des hohen Verstandes, “In praise of lofty intellect”. In the song a cuckoo and a nightingale hold a singing contest with a donkey as judge. He awards the prize to the cuckoo.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide names the bassoon fragment as derived from the setting of the Wunderhorn text Lob des hohen Verstands and prints the poem, in which the donkey awards the prize to the cuckoo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/ . The bassoon phrase stands in the opening bars of Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183.

cues.title: Rondo theme, horns
cues.text: The horn plays the rondo theme in D major, marked Allegro commodo, over open fifths held by the bassoons. The second horn enters close behind in imitation. The folk-like melody returns later as a refrain.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183: riten., Allegro commodo (Hauptzeitmass), D major, horns in imitation (the second horn’s entry marked 2.), sustained open fifths in the bassoons. Basinger: the folk-like giocoso theme is first played by the horn section over drone harmonies and recurs like a poetic refrain: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fugato in the strings, rehearsal 2
cues.text: At rehearsal 2 Mahler wrote Nicht eilen (do not hurry), and the cellos begin a running line. The basses and the other strings enter after them, p leggiero. The passage is a fugato, and each new voice enters while the earlier ones continue.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 185–186: rehearsal 2, Nicht eilen, cellos and basses with running eighths, then the successive string entries marked p leggiero. Basinger: fugal process is a chief level of organisation in the finale: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Adagietto melody in the finale
cues.text: The finale takes a melody from the Adagietto and sets it among quick string figures. Over the first violins Mahler writes schwungvoll, “with swing”.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 196 (rehearsal 8): first violins marked schwungvoll over quick string figures. Basinger: the Adagietto surfaces in the finale after the second refrain-fugue pair, transmuted into a grazioso, flowing dance: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler and the Bach edition
cues.text: While writing the Fifth, Mahler was studying Bach’s collected works, to which he subscribed. In the finale the string parts enter one after another in fugues and canons. A horn then plays a tune.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction, on the Bach edition and the finale’s contrapuntal writing. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: Change to two flats
cues.text: The key signature changes from two sharps to two flats. Mahler marks the passage Nicht eilen. (Pesante.), meaning do not hurry, weightily. The running figure of the fugue returns in violas, cellos and basses beneath staccato horns and trombones.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 224: two flats, Nicht eilen. (Pesante.), the running figure in violas, cellos and basses, staccato horns and trombones. Basinger: whenever the giocoso refrain recurs it precedes fugues on the wind motives of the introduction: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the brass chorale
cues.text: The brass chorale returns in D major at Pesante (Etwas gehalten). Horns, trumpets and trombones play broad fff chords with bells raised, a cymbal is left to ring, and strings run beneath. In the second movement the chorale dissolved back into the stormy music.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 244: Pesante (Etwas gehalten), D major, brass fff, Schalltrichter auf, Becken klingen lassen, running string figures ff sempre. Basinger: a chorale reminiscent of the second movement materializes at the high point of the finale and a gradually accelerating coda brings the Fifth to a dramatic close: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Presto coda and final chords
cues.text: The closing pages move into Presto, with chromatic runs in winds and strings. Short chords marked secco follow, and timpani, cymbals, bass drum and triangle are told to damp quickly. The symphony ends on these short chords.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 251: Presto, chromatic runs, secco chords, schnell abdämpfen in the percussion, final bars. Basinger: the gradually accelerating coda brings the Fifth to a dramatic close: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s piano roll, Leipzig, 1905
cues.text: On 9 November 1905 Mahler sat at a Welte-Mignon reproducing piano in Leipzig and recorded the symphony’s first movement, the funeral march, as a piano roll.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page for the symphony lists the 1905 Leipzig recording of Movement 1: Trauermarsch (piano): https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/

transitions.title: From oboe to horn
transitions.from: Intro · Horn, bassoon, oboe and clarinet
transitions.to: A · Horn theme and string entries, D major
transitions.how: After a riten. the horn takes the main tune at Allegro commodo (Hauptzeitmass), and a second horn follows in imitation. Beneath the tune’s falling phrases the bassoons hold D major in open fifths.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 183: riten., Allegro commodo (Hauptzeitmass), horns in imitation, open fifths in the bassoons. Basinger: the giocoso theme is first played by the horn section over drone harmonies.

transitions.title: The brass chorale in D major
transitions.from: Link · Fugues leading to the brass chorale
transitions.to: Coda · Brass chorale and closing Allegro
transitions.how: At Pesante (Etwas gehalten) the horns, trumpets and trombones make a crescendo to fff on a D-major chord, with bells raised (Schalltrichter auf), and the cymbal is left to ring (Becken klingen lassen). The strings continue their running figures underneath. At this climax a chorale appears that Basinger likened to the second movement, and the music moves into the faster coda.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 244: Pesante (Etwas gehalten), brass crescendo to fff, Schalltrichter auf, Becken klingen lassen, running strings. Basinger: a chorale reminiscent of the second movement materializes at the high point.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, V, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed p. 183: horn and woodwind introduction; pp. 185–186: string fugato; p. 210: horn and string melody; pp. 244–251: brass chorale and closing pages.

timeline.note: A horn note sets off short replies from bassoon, oboe and clarinet.
The horn plays the rondo tune above woodwinds and low strings.
Cellos start the fugato; other string sections take up the running line.
The horn and strings play longer phrases above held notes in the woodwind.
The brass play the chorale over running strings and the full orchestra.
Fast orchestral figures lead to the short closing chords.
The written finale closes in D major.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
